The way that this usually happens with a startup is that they take money from a VC firm in exchange for a LOT of control over the product (voting power, ability to appoint leadership, etc).That's how you end up with things like Reddit, where the investors want a huge return and want to control the message.

With a more distributed ownership chain, it will be MUCH harder for something like this to happen.

Here are a few of the conditions that VC companies impose on new startups. Young and inexperienced people might be unaware of this and think of VC as just free money. It is anything but.

  1. Mandatory exit. Venture capitalists are in it just for the money. VC will set a time frame and will cash out at the end of that term. For Reddit that was 10 years. You didn't think all this was just coincidence with their 10th anniversary did you? Their celebration video looks exactly like a pitch for an ad platform.

  2. Loss of independence You may still be the chief executive officer, but you answer to the board now and it's not just your company anymore. The VCs will ask for one or more board seats and the right to veto key decisions and control the firm's capital structure.

  3. They will have the right to fire you and your management team. You could find yourself reporting to a new CEO, or be ousted from the company you founded. This is how Yishan was burnt out and parted ways.

  4. Anti-dilution protection. If the company's stock price goes down any time in the future, they get additional stock for free.

  5. Dividends. In addition to stock, they get a guaranteed rate of return.

  6. Liquidation preferences. VCs get their principal and dividends back before anyone else gets a penny.

  7. Participating preferred. They get to double dip—they first get their investment plus dividends, then the value of their stock.

  8. Mandatory redemption. This requires the company to buy their stock back by a certain date, establishing a deadline for an exit event.

  9. Demand registration rights. The VCs can force the company to file a registration statement with the Securities and Exchange Commission to initiate an initial public offering—another way of forcing an exit event. Reddit is not big enough for this to be worthwhile.

  10. Approval rights. The VCs must approve any new financings and have the right to participate.

  11. Reps and warranties. You'll also have to accept personal liability for representations you've made about key aspects of the company. They will have the right to sue you for all you own if you forgot to give them any bad news.

[source]

We can all see how all of these played a part in the demise of Reddit. It is now owned and commandeered by the same outfit that publishes GQ and Bride magazine, go figure.

Up until a few weeks ago, you wouldn't have been able to (assuming you're not extremely wealthy). The big thing about the rule changes that come from the JOBS Act are:

  1. A startup can advertise that they are seeking investment money publicly (they could not do this before).
  2. A startup can take investment money without having to do an IPO (could certainly do this before, but it was much harder).
  3. Individuals with a net worth lower than $1 million or that make less than $250,000 per year can now invest in startup companies (this was, amazingly, illegal up until now; talk about the rich getting richer).

As I said, the final part of this (the third point) JUST went into effect a few weeks ago. If Voat really wanted to get some additional media attention, they should hook up with a crowd-funding company like Indiegogo that has expressed interest in this process (Kickstarter has stated they have no intentions of doing this) and use this as a great kick-off event. There's no way it could fail (with so many people exiting from Reddit) from a financing standpoint, and both companies would get huge additional exposure in places they otherwise wouldn't (think business media outlets like Forbes, etc).

Even Angel Investors are looking for a return, they just tend to be ok with taking a bigger risk on ideas. The only way you're going to see true altruistic investment is with equity crowd-sourcing. If you're a VC or AI the minimum amount you're going to come to the table with is five-figures, and that's out of the reach of almost every user on this website. Conversely, with equity crowd-sourcing, investments can be as small as $100, which a much larger portion of the Voat userbase would be willing to invest.

Crowd sourcing will not work for a platform like this unless there is a de facto subscription based system because of the lurking content and the periodic waves of attention Voat will get. There are VCs who can share your vision; when I founded my current company I had a VC who not only agreed with the business plan but also with the ideas and the motives behind the plan that many before did not agree on.
